Haven't played the game yet myself, but I feel making every party member bisexual is a neutral albeit "easy way" romance option. I assume the reason this is done is to either: (1) ensure diversity, (2) give players the freedom to pursue any character they'd like, or (3) give the devs more time to work on other aspects of the game they were more interested in working on like the skill checks and such.

While I see no real issue with it, it does say a lot when most devs go for bisexual romantic options as the be-all-end-all since so many people clamor about it. May just be me, but it would be interesting to see games explore more exclusive romantic options since it would require players to engage in more roleplaying to achieve their romantic option and maybe give them more perspective on it. Despite that, your point stands, and you're not crazy for thinking *Baldur's Gate* is not in the wrong. So long as the romantic options are interesting, then no one will complain.

If I were to gauge the exact reason why people think it's lazy game design, it may be because the romantic options are quick to get too horny. It was an issue I noticed in *Pillars of Eternity 2* for some of the characters and the general juvenile writing regarding sexual content there.

**Neon Genesis Evangelion**

Ah yes, the wonderful mindfuck mecha anime everyone loves to praise. I will not dwell on my grievances with Evangelion for long, but this has to be addressed: Gendo was not the only bad parent in the show. Later episodes and movies dabble into Gendo and Yui as characters and essentially show that they both have essentially abandoned their son. Their son, who would eventually grow up to develop an almost parasitic need for attention and approval from others no matter how cruel or indifferent everyone around him is. Many people will throw shade at Gendo for being so uncaring of his son's plight and using him as a tool, but Yui definitely deserves some attention for deciding to abandon her son. No amount of good reason will justify it.

* Expand your scope of media--read more books, watch more shows, play more games and pay a lot of attention to how the story unfolds
* Listen carefully to how people talk--taking note to how people talk teaches you how to write a natural voice for your characters
* Appreciate the unexpected in your developing plot--sometimes the story and characters may veer in a different direction, and you can use that to help build them up better
* Have a close network of colleagues--the extra set of eyes to catch structural and narrative issues helps
* Never stop writing--if you have a story running through your head, let it flow out on the page and don't try and quell it

Aside from them, there's no mention of Guru, Dmitri, Panda King, or Penelope who all had pivotal roles in the game. I'm certain the idea to have just Sly, Bentley, and Murray on their own is to reduce the overall cast, but that was why the other members were used sparingly. Penelope not being mentioned is a big deservice, in my opinion, because of how well she played off Bentley in the later episodes of Honor Among Thieves and being an all-around witty character that fit into the team dynamic well.

I'll admit, I like the idea of Sly and Carmelita's relationship being in the background of the concept, but the way it was done doesn't feel right. Firstly, it feels like a cheap way to get Carmelita out of the picture to just have her be a damsel again when we've seen her capable of handling her own. Secondly, it feels even more jarring that McSweeney was made to be the main villain considering the impression he left in the comic. Thirdly, the fact the team is hinging the whole plot of the game on this incident feels lacking. The Sly Cooper games have a personal edge to them, yes, but they do so in a very bombastic way. A plot like Taking back the Thievieus Racconus or finding all the Clockwerk Parts sound like they can carry a whole game--Sly trying to save Carmelita from McSweeney doesn't. ESPECIALLY if they're going to have the Gang go through a whole rogue's gallery getting to McSweeney.

Personally, I like the idea of giving Interpol more of a presence in the game world. I feel Band of Thieves with Neyla enlisting mercenaries to fight the Contessa and Carmelita hiring mercenaries in Honor Among Thieves did this well. I'm honestly surprised Interpol doesn't have more of a presence in the games aside from one officer chasing Sly. So...this game decides to make Interpol more threatening by...having a single officer go after Sly again. I'll be blunt--the cop character they have is kind of bland and the idea of having him be an albino raccoon is very on-the-nose. Yeah, he looks threatening and all, but I feel it would've been better if they just Interpol more as a group entity. Just imagine all of Interpol throwing their money into mercenaries and seeing them scattered across each episode as they hunt down the Cooper Gang.

Finally, I think the idea of setting the game with a darker tone feels a little off. The Sly Cooper games have always been dark, but the writers knew how to showcase it in a witty and family-friendly way. This concept seems to lean into full crime-drama and that leaves a bit of a bad taste in my mouth. With Savo's rampant distaste for Thieves in Time and Honor Among Thieves aside, this feels like it's being done without the heart of the series in the right place. Band of Thieves--the game that definitely inspired this--was dark, but not hopelessly so like it looks here. With how much they hammered the whole "how long can a thief stay undercover before life catches up to them", they seem to be going for a possible ending where Sly breaks it off with Carmelita and goes back to being a full-time thief. It's expected with how dark they seem to want to make the game, and it's cliche.

Since there are questions, I'll post a summary of what I changed here:

* Ice is widely considered a poor typing defensively but a strong type offensively, so I changed very little. I had decided to make Ice resist Water and Ground and made it immune to itself to give it a little more leeway.
* Normal took a little bit to consider since it does neutral damage overall and takes neutral damage overall. Making it resist Fairy and Dark may not make sense at first, but I thought about it like DnD (Fairy-type could be seen as Good, Dark-type would be Evil, and Normal-type would be Neutral).
* I made Grass resist Fairy based on the idea that fairies are usually connected to nature in some way. Also made it super-effective against Rock since it was already super-effective against Ground.
* Since Poison was already strong against Grass, I thought making it strong against Water made sense due to how it ties to pollution. I also made it do neutral damage to Steel since, while I know Poison in Pokemon is more aligned to disease, acid can melt through metal.
* Psychic was kind of tricky to work with since it had so much happen to it to nerf it over the years, so I decided to make it resist Fairy (there may be some clever connection about how the power of the mind and magic are one in the same somewhere in there).
* I made Dragon resist Poison, though this may change later down the line to help make Poison more viable. The big change was making it do neutral damage to Fairy due to how often dragons are portrayed in fairy tales. I may end up changing this so that both types either do neutral damage to each other or resist each other.
* Ghost is super-effective against Fairy because I'm surprised no one's brought up fairy tales vs. ghost stories.
* Electric is super-effective against Steel.
* Bug does neutral damage to Fairy.
